chapter_note.about: The Karnaugh map is a truth table arranged so that neighbouring cells differ in one variable, which turns the algebra rule xy + xy' = x into a picture. This chapter covers the Gray-code layout and adjacency, the grouping rule, don't-care cells, prime and essential implicants, minimal sum of products and minimal product of sums, the Quine-McCluskey table that does the same job without a map, the cost of the result in literals and gates, and hazard-free covers. GATE gives a minterm list or a map and asks for the minimal expression, often with several tied correct options.
chapter_note.simple: A Karnaugh map is a picture of a truth table where cells next to each other differ by one switch, so terms that can be merged are easy to spot. You circle neighbouring 1s in rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16, and each circle gives a short formula. Cells marked 'do not care' can join a circle if that helps. The biggest circles are the prime implicants, and the ones you cannot avoid are the essential ones. Circling the 0s instead gives the product-of-sums form, and a table method does the same without a picture. In a real circuit you sometimes add an extra circle to avoid a brief glitch.

cards.title: Gray-code layout and adjacency
cards.simple: A Karnaugh map is a truth table folded into a grid so that neighbouring cells are almost the same. Two cells are neighbours when their inputs differ in exactly one switch. To make that work, the labels along the sides do not count in the usual order 00, 01, 10, 11. They go 00, 01, 11, 10, so that each label differs from the next in just one bit. The grid also wraps around like the screen of an old video game: leave on the right and you come back on the left, leave at the top and you come back at the bottom. In exam words: K-map rows and columns follow Gray code (00, 01, 11, 10); adjacent cells differ in one variable and the edges wrap around; read the minterm number from the labels, not by counting cells.
cards.idea: A K-map places minterms so that cells next to each other differ in **one variable**. Rows and columns are labelled in **Gray code** (00, 01, 11, 10) and the edges **wrap around**. Read the minterm number from the labels, never by counting cells.
cards.definition:
- For 4 variables $A,B,C,D$: rows are $AB$ and columns are $CD$, both in the order 00, 01, 11, 10.
- The cell at row $AB$ and column $CD$ is the minterm $m=8A+4B+2C+D$.
- Two cells are adjacent exactly when their minterm numbers differ in one bit. Each cell has $n$ neighbours in an $n$-variable map.
- The map wraps: the top row is adjacent to the bottom row, and the left column to the right column.
cards.intuition_full: Gray code is an ordering of bit patterns in which each pattern differs from the next in exactly one bit: 00, 01, 11, 10. If you used plain binary order (00, 01, 10, 11), the step from 01 to 10 would change two bits, and cells that look adjacent would not be neighbours in the logic sense. Adjacent cells matter because two minterms that differ in one variable can be merged: xy + xy' = x. The K-map is built so that this merge becomes a picture: a pair of neighbouring ones is a group, and the changing variable drops out. The last label, 10, differs from the first, 00, in one bit as well, which is why the edges wrap: the map is really a torus. A consequence is that every cell has exactly n neighbours (one per variable), and even the four corner cells of a 4-variable map form a connected 2×2 block through the wrap-around.

examples.setup: On a 4-variable map (rows AB, columns CD), find minterm 9 and list all its neighbours.
steps: Labels run 00, 01, 11, 10 along both sides, and the cell at row AB, column CD is minterm 8A + 4B + 2C + D.
Minterm 9 = 1001: A = 1, B = 0, C = 0, D = 1. That is row 10 and column 01.
Neighbours differ in one bit. Flip B: 1101 = 13 (row 11, column 01, directly above). Flip A: 0001 = 1 (row 00, column 01). That cell lies across the top-bottom wrap.
Flip C: 1011 = 11 (row 10, column 11, to the right). Flip D: 1000 = 8 (row 10, column 00, to the left).
So minterm 9 has exactly four neighbours: 1, 8, 11, 13. The map wraps top to bottom and left to right.
examples.answer: Minterm 9 sits at row 10, column 01. Its neighbours are 1, 8, 11 and 13.

examples.setup: Which minterm is in row 01, column 10 of a 4-variable map? List its four neighbours.
steps: Row 01 means A = 0, B = 1. Column 10 means C = 1, D = 0.
The cell is 0110 = 6.
Flip A: 1110 = 14 (row 11, column 10, below). Flip B: 0010 = 2 (row 00, column 10, above).
Flip C: 0100 = 4 (row 01, column 00). This cell is on the opposite edge, so it is a wrap-around neighbour. Flip D: 0111 = 7 (row 01, column 11, left).
Trap avoided: the cells at the two ends of a row look far apart but are neighbours; row 01 is not 'next to' 10 until you read the Gray labels.
examples.answer: Minterm 6; neighbours 2, 4, 7 and 14.

examples.setup: On a 3-variable map (row A, columns BC in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10), are minterms 1 and 2 adjacent? Are 0 and 2?
steps: Minterm 1 = 001 is in column 01. Minterm 2 = 010 is in column 10. Minterm 0 = 000 is in column 00.
1 and 2 differ in two bits (001 against 010), so they are not adjacent. They sit at columns 01 and 10, which are not neighbours in the Gray order.
0 and 2 differ in one bit (000 against 010), so they are adjacent. Column 10 wraps around to column 00.
With plain binary labels (00, 01, 10, 11) the cells for 1 and 2 would have looked adjacent, which is wrong.
examples.answer: 1 and 2: not adjacent. 0 and 2: adjacent through the wrap-around.

cards.title: Grouping rule
cards.simple: Once you can see which cells are neighbours, you circle groups of 1s. A group must be a rectangle holding 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells, never 3 or 6. A bigger group gives a shorter term, because every time you double the group one more variable drops out. Inside a group some variables keep the same value on every cell, and those are the ones that show up in the term. The variables that change from cell to cell disappear. In exam words: group 2^k adjacent ones in a rectangle (wrap-around allowed); the product term keeps the n − k variables that stay constant, plain if they are 1 and complemented if they are 0.
cards.idea: Circle rectangles of **$2^k$ adjacent ones** (1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells, wrap-around allowed). The term for a group keeps only the variables that **stay constant** inside it, which is $n-k$ literals. Bigger groups give fewer literals.
cards.definition:
- A group is a rectangle of $2^k$ cells that are all 1 (or X). It may wrap around the edges.
- A group of $2^k$ cells in an $n$-variable map gives a product term with $n-k$ literals.
- A variable that is 1 on every cell appears plain; one that is 0 on every cell appears complemented; a variable that changes is dropped.
- $F$ is the OR of the terms of the chosen groups, and every 1 must be covered.
cards.intuition_full: Grouping is the picture of the algebra rule xy + xy' = x. Two neighbouring ones differ in one variable, so that variable cancels. Two such pairs that are neighbours cancel a second variable, and so on, which is why group sizes are powers of 2: each doubling removes exactly one variable. A group of 3 or 6 cells would not correspond to any single product term, so it is not allowed. To read the term, look at the labels around the group. A label bit that is the same for every cell of the group is part of the term, and a bit that varies is dropped. Overlapping groups are allowed and often useful, because a cell may belong to a bigger group even if another group already covers it. Wrap-around groups are the usual surprise: cells on opposite edges are neighbours, so a pair of columns at the two ends forms a legal group.

examples.setup: Group the ones of F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(4, 6, 12, 13, 14) and write the minimal SOP.
steps: Mark the ones: cells 4 and 12 are in column 00, cells 6 and 14 are in column 10, and 13 is in row 11, column 01.
Cells 4, 6, 12, 14 form a 2×2 block when the map wraps left to right (column 10 is next to column 00).
Read the block: B is 1 on all four cells and D is 0 on all four. A and C change. The term is BD′, with 4 − 2 = 2 literals.
Cell 13 is left over. Pair it with 12: they differ only in D. A = 1, B = 1, C = 0 stay fixed, so the term is ABC′ (3 literals).
F = BD′ + ABC′, which has 5 literals. The block of 4 is cheaper per cell than the pair.
examples.answer: F = BD′ + ABC′.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 4, 5, 10, 11, 14, 15). Find the minimal SOP, and decide whether A′C′ + AC + BD is a correct cover.
steps: Cells 0, 1, 4, 5 form a 2×2 block at the top left: A = 0 and C = 0 stay fixed. The term is A′C′.
Cells 10, 11, 14, 15 form a 2×2 block at the bottom right: A = 1 and C = 1 stay fixed. The term is AC.
F = A′C′ + AC, with 4 literals.
Test the option A′C′ + AC + BD. The term BD covers cells 5, 7, 13 and 15. Cell 7 is a 0 of F, so this option covers a zero and is wrong.
Trap avoided: a cover must include every 1 and no 0. Finding one wrongly covered 0 rejects an option quickly.
examples.answer: F = A′C′ + AC (4 literals). The option with BD is wrong.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(5, 7, 13). The three ones form an L-shape. Can you group all three?
steps: Cells 5 and 7 are neighbours (row 01, columns 01 and 11). Cells 5 and 13 are neighbours (column 01, rows 01 and 11).
Three cells cannot form a group, because group sizes are 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16.
Use two overlapping pairs. {5, 7}: A = 0, B = 1, D = 1 fixed, so A′BD. {5, 13}: B = 1, C = 0, D = 1 fixed, so BC′D.
F = A′BD + BC′D, with 6 literals. Overlap on cell 5 is allowed.
examples.answer: F = A′BD + BC′D.

edge_cases: A group of 16 cells gives the constant 1 (no literals).
Groups may overlap; a cell can be covered twice.
Wrap-around groups are valid, including the four corners.
A single isolated 1 gives a full minterm with n literals.

cards.title: Don't-care cells
cards.simple: Sometimes a problem says 'we do not care what the output is for these inputs', because those inputs can never happen, or the answer there does not matter. Those cells are marked X. They are a free bonus. If treating an X as a 1 lets you circle a bigger group, do it. If an X does not help, ignore it, because you never have to cover it. One X can be counted as a 1 in one group and left out of everything else. In exam words: a don't-care may be used as 1 to enlarge a group but need not be covered; the minimal SOP covers every 1 and as many X cells as help.
cards.idea: A **don't-care** (X) is a free choice. Treat it as **1** when that makes a group bigger, and ignore it otherwise. The groups must cover every real 1 but **never need to cover** an X.
cards.definition:
- Inputs that cannot occur, or whose output is unconstrained, are written $d(\dots)$ or marked X.
- Group the 1s, using X cells as 1s wherever that enlarges a group.
- Every 1 must be covered. An X may be covered or left uncovered.
- Using X cells never increases the literal count; it can only keep it or lower it.
- Don't-cares add prime implicants but never make one essential.
cards.intuition_full: An X means the specification does not say what the output should be there, so the designer can choose 0 or 1, whichever gives the cheapest circuit. In grouping terms, an X is a wildcard: it can join a group as a 1, or it can stay outside. You pick whichever choice gives larger groups and therefore shorter terms. You are never forced to cover an X, so an X cell that sits alone does not need its own term. Different groups can treat the same X differently, but the final circuit gives it one output. A common point of confusion is that an X is not a 1 that must be covered. Another is thinking that X cells can create an essential prime implicant: an essential implicant is defined by a real 1 that only it covers, and an X never counts as a real 1.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(2, 4, 5, 7, 10) with don't-cares d(6, 8, 11, 14). Find the minimal SOP.
steps: Mark the ones at 2, 4, 5, 7, 10 and the X cells at 6, 8, 11, 14.
Group the whole column CD = 10 (cells 2, 6, 14, 10). The X cells at 6 and 14 are used as 1s. Constant: C = 1, D = 0. Term CD′.
Group the whole row AB = 01 (cells 4, 5, 7, 6). The X at 6 is used again. Constant: A = 0, B = 1. Term A′B.
The X cells at 8 and 11 are not needed. Leave them uncovered.
F = CD′ + A′B, with 4 literals. Treating every X as 0 would cost 9 literals.
examples.answer: F = CD′ + A′B.

examples.setup: A BCD digit detector (inputs A B C D give a decimal digit 0 to 9). Output F = 1 for digits 5 to 9. Inputs 10 to 15 never occur. Find the minimal SOP.
steps: The group A = 1 covers cells 8 to 15: the ones 8, 9 and six don't-cares. Term A (1 literal).
Cells 5 and 7 with the don't-cares 13 and 15 form a group where B = 1, D = 1: term BD.
Cells 6 and 7 with the don't-cares 14 and 15 form a group where B = 1, C = 1: term BC.
F = A + BD + BC, with 5 literals. Without don't-cares, the same function would need more.
examples.answer: F = A + BD + BC.

examples.setup: In the digit-detector example, what is the cost if every don't-care is treated as 0?
steps: With X as 0 the function is F = Σm(5, 6, 7, 8, 9) only.
Pairs: {5, 7} gives A′BD; {6, 7} gives A′BC; {8, 9} gives AB′C′. These cover all five ones.
F = A′BD + A′BC + AB′C′, with 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 literals.
With don't-cares the cost was 5 literals. Don't-cares are free simplification.
examples.answer: 9 literals, against 5 when the don't-cares are used.

cards.why: Real specifications have impossible or irrelevant inputs, and don't-cares turn them into cheaper circuits. In GATE: minimise a function that includes d-cells and choose the right option.
how: Mark 1s, 0s and X cells on the map.
Treat an X as 1 only if it enlarges a group.
Make sure every real 1 is covered; do not insist on covering the Xs.
Read the terms, and count literals as usual.
cards.mistake: Covering every X, or adding a term just for an X. Xs are optional. Another slip is treating an X as a 0 that blocks a group; it is a wildcard that helps.
edge_cases: An X can be used in several groups; the final circuit fixes it to one value.
If no X enlarges a group, the answer is the same as without them.
X cells never make a prime implicant essential.
In a POS problem, an X can be used as 0 to enlarge a group of zeros.
connections: Groups themselves: card k2. Which groups are essential: card k4.
BCD and other codes with unused patterns are a typical source (dl.comb).
Foundations: **Sets and logic** (found.sets_logic) covers the idea of cases that are 'unspecified' rather than true or false.

A **don't-care** (X) is a free choice. Treat it as **1** when that makes a group bigger, and ignore it otherwise. The groups must cover every real 1 but **never need to cover** an X.

- Inputs that cannot occur, or whose output is unconstrained, are written $d(\dots)$ or marked X.
- Group the 1s, using X cells as 1s wherever that enlarges a group.
- Every 1 must be covered. An X may be covered or left uncovered.
- Using X cells never increases the literal count; it can only keep it or lower it.
- Don't-cares add prime implicants but never make one essential.

**Worked example.** F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(2, 4, 5, 7, 10) with don't-cares d(6, 8, 11, 14). Find the minimal SOP.

1. Mark the ones at 2, 4, 5, 7, 10 and the X cells at 6, 8, 11, 14.
2. Group the whole column CD = 10 (cells 2, 6, 14, 10). The X cells at 6 and 14 are used as 1s. Constant: C = 1, D = 0. Term CD′.
3. Group the whole row AB = 01 (cells 4, 5, 7, 6). The X at 6 is used again. Constant: A = 0, B = 1. Term A′B.
4. The X cells at 8 and 11 are not needed. Leave them uncovered.
5. F = CD′ + A′B, with 4 literals. Treating every X as 0 would cost 9 literals.

**Answer:** F = CD′ + A′B.
cards.why_full:
Real specifications have impossible or irrelevant inputs, and don't-cares turn them into cheaper circuits. In GATE: minimise a function that includes d-cells and choose the right option.

cards.title: Prime and essential prime implicants
cards.simple: A prime implicant is a group of 1s that cannot be made any bigger, so it is already as large as it can be. Some of these groups cannot be avoided, because they cover a 1 that no other maximal group touches. Those are the essential prime implicants, and every cheapest answer must include them. The other prime implicants are optional: you only use some of them if there are 1s left over. To find the essentials, take each 1 in turn and count how many maximal groups contain it. If the count is exactly one, that group is essential. In exam words: a prime implicant (PI) is a group that cannot be enlarged; an essential PI covers at least one 1 that no other PI covers.
cards.idea: A **prime implicant** (PI) is a group of 1s that cannot grow. An **essential** PI covers a 1 that **no other PI covers**, so every minimal SOP contains it. A non-essential PI is optional.
cards.definition:
- Implicant: a product term whose cells are all 1 (or X). Prime implicant: an implicant that is not contained in a larger implicant.
- Essential PI: there is a real 1 (not an X) that lies in this PI and in no other PI.
- Minimal SOP = all essential PIs + a cheapest set of other PIs covering the remaining 1s.
- Counting recipe: list all PIs, then test every 1 for the number of PIs that contain it.
cards.intuition_full: Grouping as large as possible gives the prime implicants. A smaller group is always wasteful, because a larger group exists that does the same job with fewer literals, so a minimal cover uses only primes. Among the primes, a 1 that sits in a single prime forces that prime into every cover: nothing else could cover it. That makes the prime essential. After all the essentials are chosen, some 1s may remain uncovered, and non-essential primes are used for them. A prime that overlaps entirely with the essentials is redundant and does not appear in the minimal answer. Don't-cares are treated as 1 when finding primes (they can make a group larger) but they never count as a 1 that needs covering, so they cannot make a prime essential. This is why counting essentials with don't-cares is a classic trap.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 3, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15). Find all prime implicants and decide which are essential.
steps: Mark the ones: 0, 1, 3 (top row), 10, 11, 14, 15 and 13.
Maximal groups (prime implicants): A′B′C′ (0, 1), A′B′D (1, 3), B′CD (3, 11), AC (10, 11, 14, 15) and ABD (13, 15). None can grow. That makes 5 PIs.
Essential: m0 is only in A′B′C′, m10 and m14 are only in AC, and m13 is only in ABD. So A′B′C′, AC and ABD are essential.
A′B′D and B′CD both cover m3, and each other cell they cover is covered elsewhere, so neither is essential.
Count: 5 PIs, 3 essential. The essentials cover everything except m3, which either A′B′D or B′CD can supply: 11 literals.
examples.answer: 5 prime implicants, 3 essential (A′B′C′, AC, ABD).

examples.setup: F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 7). How many prime implicants are there, and how many are essential?
steps: Cells 0, 1, 2, 3 form the row A = 0: prime implicant A′.
Cells 3 and 7 form the pair BC (A varies): prime implicant BC.
No other group is maximal: A′ cannot grow (A = 1 has only m7 as a 1) and BC cannot grow.
Essential: m0, m1, m2 are only in A′, and m7 is only in BC. Both are essential.
Count: 2 PIs, 2 essential. Minimal SOP: A′ + BC (3 literals).
examples.answer: 2 prime implicants, both essential.

examples.setup: Cyclic case: F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7). How many PIs and how many essential?
steps: Pairs of adjacent ones: (0,1) A′B′, (1,3) A′C, (3,7) BC, (7,6) AB, (6,4) AC′, (4,0) B′C′. All 6 are prime.
Each 1 lies in exactly two of them (for example m1 in A′B′ and A′C). So no 1 has a single owner.
No prime is essential.
Two minimal covers of 3 terms each exist: {A′B′, BC, AC′} and {A′C, AB, B′C′}.
examples.answer: 6 prime implicants, 0 essential.

Don't-cares add PIs but never make one essential.
Every essential PI is prime, but not every prime is essential.
A PI whose 1s are all covered by essentials is redundant.

cards.title: Minimal sum of products
cards.simple: Finding the cheapest answer is a three-step recipe. First, list the biggest possible groups. Second, take the unavoidable ones (the essentials), because every answer needs them. Third, look at the 1s that are still uncovered, and pick the fewest, biggest groups that cover them. Sometimes two or three different choices cost exactly the same, and then the exam can list each of them as a correct answer. In exam words: minimal SOP = all essential prime implicants plus a cheapest set of other prime implicants that covers the remaining 1s; several covers may tie.
cards.idea: **Minimal SOP** = all **essential** prime implicants + the cheapest set of other primes that covers the remaining 1s. Several covers can have the same cost, and then each is a correct minimal answer.
cards.definition:
Recipe on a K-map:

1. List every prime implicant.
2. Take the essential ones.
3. Mark the 1s they cover. Choose the fewest primes (then fewest literals) that cover the rest.
4. OR the terms.

- Cost is the total number of literals (ties broken by number of terms).
- When two covers tie, both are correct minimal SOPs.
cards.intuition_full: Minimisation is a covering problem: choose terms so that every 1 is covered while the total number of literals is as small as possible. Primes are enough to consider, because replacing any term by a prime that contains it never raises the cost. Essentials must be taken, so after step 2 the problem only involves the leftover ones. The leftover problem is often small, a few cells that can be covered in several ways. There the choice is genuinely open: two covers can cost the same, and then no one answer is 'the' minimal SOP. GATE exploits this by listing several correct options in a multiple-select question. The way to check an option is to see that it covers all the 1s, covers no 0, and has the minimal literal count. Overlapping primes are normal; a cell covered twice costs nothing.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 14). Find the minimal SOP and say how many minimal covers there are.
steps: The ones sit at 1, 3 (top row), 4, 5, 6 (row 01), 10 and 14.
Essential primes: m3 lies only in A′B′D (cells 1, 3), and m10 lies only in ACD′ (cells 10, 14). Take both. They cover 1, 3, 10, 14.
Leftover ones: 4, 5, 6. Possible primes for them: A′BC′ (4, 5), A′BD′ (4, 6), BCD′ (6, 14) and A′C′D (1, 5).
Cheapest cover of 4, 5, 6 needs 2 more primes, each with 3 literals: {A′BC′, A′BD′}, {A′BC′, BCD′} or {A′C′D, A′BD′}.
All three covers cost 3 × 4 = 12 literals, so F has three correct minimal SOPs. One of them: F = A′B′D + ACD′ + A′BC′ + A′BD′.
examples.answer: 12 literals; three tied minimal covers, e.g. A′B′D + ACD′ + A′BC′ + A′BD′.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 15). Find the minimal SOP, and say whether A′B′ + BC + AC is a valid minimal answer.
steps: Cells 0, 1, 2, 3 are the row AB = 00: prime A′B′. Cells 6, 7, 14, 15 are the 2×2 block with B = 1, C = 1: prime BC.
Both are essential (cell 0 only in A′B′, cell 6 only in BC), and together they cover all eight ones.
F = A′B′ + BC, with 4 literals.
Test A′B′ + BC + AC: the term AC covers cells 10, 11, 14, 15, but cells 10 and 11 are zeros of F. So it is wrong.
Trap avoided: a longer cover is not 'safe'. Extra terms must not cover any zero.
examples.answer: F = A′B′ + BC (4 literals). The option with AC is wrong.

examples.setup: Why does the choice of the leftover cover matter when two options tie, and how do you check an option quickly?
steps: Take the basic example: after the essentials, {A′BC′, A′BD′} and {A′C′D, A′BD′} both cover 4, 5, 6 at the same cost.
A multiple-select question may list both as correct. Do not stop at the first minimal cover you find.

An option with an extra redundant term has more than 12 literals: it covers correctly but is not minimal.
examples.answer: Verify every option by coverage and cost; ties mean several correct answers.

cards.title: Minimal product of sums
cards.simple: Sometimes the answer must be written as a product of sums (POS), which is a set of brackets joined by AND, each bracket holding ORs. The trick is to look at the 0s instead of the 1s. Circle the 0s exactly the way you circle 1s. That gives a formula for 'the function is 0', which is the opposite of what you want. So flip it with De Morgan's law: complement the formula, and the brackets of sums appear. In exam words: group the zeros to get F′ as an SOP, then complement using De Morgan's laws to get the POS of F; each zero-group becomes a sum with the variables complemented.
cards.idea: For a **product of sums**, group the **0s**. Read the groups as an SOP for $\bar F$, then **complement** it with De Morgan: each group of zeros becomes one sum term with the complemented variables.
cards.definition:
1. Group the 0 cells exactly as you would group 1s (powers of 2, wrap-around, don't-cares as 0 if they help).
2. Read an SOP for $\bar F$ from the groups.
3. Complement: $F=\overline{\bar F}$. By De Morgan, each product term $xy'z$ becomes the sum $(x'+y+z')$.

- A group of $2^k$ zeros gives a sum term with $n-k$ literals.
- Literal count of the minimal POS = literal count of the minimal SOP of $\bar F$.
cards.intuition_full: A POS says 'F is 1 only when every bracket is satisfied', so it is natural to find F by finding where it is 0. Each zero of F has to make at least one bracket false. Grouping zeros is the same problem as grouping ones for the complement function F′, which is why the technique is identical. The flip at the end is De Morgan: if F′ = BD + AC then F = (BD + AC)′ = (BD)′ (AC)′ = (B′ + D′)(A′ + C′). Each group of zeros produces one bracket, with each variable replaced by its complement. A product of sums is not the same as the SOP rewritten: it may have fewer or more literals, so a question that asks for one form must be answered in that form. The common slip is to group the wrong value, or to forget to complement the variables in the brackets.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12). Find the minimal product of sums.
steps: Group the zeros 5, 7, 13, 15: a 2×2 block where B = 1 and D = 1 stay fixed. Product term BD.
Group the zeros 10, 11, 14, 15: a 2×2 block where A = 1 and C = 1 stay fixed. Product term AC.
These two groups cover all seven zeros, so F′ = BD + AC. Complement with De Morgan: F = (BD + AC)′ = (B′ + D′)(A′ + C′).
Check m5 (a zero): (B′ + D′) = 0 + 0 = 0, so F = 0 ✓. Check m4 (a one): (B′ + D′) = 0 + 1 = 1 and (A′ + C′) = 1, so F = 1 ✓.
examples.answer: F = (B′ + D′)(A′ + C′), with 4 literals.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 3). Write the minimal SOP and the minimal POS and compare their literals.
steps: SOP: pairs {0, 1} gives A′B′ and {1, 3} gives A′C. F = A′B′ + A′C, with 4 literals.
POS: group the zeros. {4, 5, 6, 7} is the row A = 1: term A. {2, 6} has B = 1, C = 0: term BC′. So F′ = A + BC′.
Complement: F = A′(B′ + C), with 3 literals.
The POS is shorter here. Check m1 (a one): A′ = 1 and (B′ + C) = 1 + 1 = 1 ✓.
examples.answer: SOP: A′B′ + A′C (4 literals). POS: A′(B′ + C) (3 literals).

examples.setup: Why is the POS not simply the SOP with brackets moved around, for the function in the basic example?
steps: The minimal SOP of the same F is C′D′ + B′C′ + A′D′ + A′B′: four terms, 8 literals.
The minimal POS (B′ + D′)(A′ + C′) has only 4 literals.
The two forms come from different groupings: ones for the SOP, zeros for the POS.
So the form asked for decides which cells to group.
examples.answer: SOP has 8 literals and POS has 4. Group the value that matches the required form.

**Worked example.** F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12). Find the minimal product of sums.

1. Mark the ones at 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12. The zeros are 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15.
2. Group the zeros 5, 7, 13, 15: a 2×2 block where B = 1 and D = 1 stay fixed. Product term BD.
3. Group the zeros 10, 11, 14, 15: a 2×2 block where A = 1 and C = 1 stay fixed. Product term AC.
4. These two groups cover all seven zeros, so F′ = BD + AC. Complement with De Morgan: F = (BD + AC)′ = (B′ + D′)(A′ + C′).
5. Check m5 (a zero): (B′ + D′) = 0 + 0 = 0, so F = 0 ✓. Check m4 (a one): (B′ + D′) = 0 + 1 = 1 and (A′ + C′) = 1, so F = 1 ✓.

**Answer:** F = (B′ + D′)(A′ + C′), with 4 literals.

cards.title: Quine-McCluskey tabular method
cards.simple: Quine-McCluskey is the K-map done as a table, so it works for any number of variables and a computer can do it. First write each minterm in binary and sort the list by how many 1s each has. Two terms can be merged if they differ in exactly one bit, and you write the merged term with a dash in that place. Keep merging the new terms until nothing merges. Any term that could not be merged any further is a prime implicant. At the end a small chart shows which prime implicants are really needed. In exam words: group minterms by number of 1s, merge pairs that differ in one bit (dash in that place), repeat; terms that never merge are the prime implicants; a covering chart picks the essentials.
cards.idea: **Quine-McCluskey** finds the prime implicants by table. **Group** minterms by their number of 1s, **merge** pairs that differ in one bit (writing a dash there), and repeat. Terms that **never merge** are prime, and a chart then picks the essentials.
cards.definition:
1. Write each minterm in binary; sort into groups by the number of 1s.
2. Compare each term with those in the next group. If they differ in exactly one bit, merge them: put a dash in that bit. Mark both as used.
3. Repeat on the merged list (dashes must be in the same places) until no merge is possible.
4. Unused (unmerged) terms are the prime implicants.
5. Build a chart of primes against minterms; a column with one mark gives an essential prime.

A dash means the variable is dropped.
cards.intuition_full: Merging two terms that differ in one bit is the same as xy + xy' = x: the differing variable drops out, and we write a dash for it. Only terms in adjacent groups can differ in one bit, because their counts of 1s differ by exactly 1, so the table only compares neighbouring groups; that is why the grouping step saves work. A merged term covers all the minterms of its parents. After a round, terms that were used are not prime because a larger term replaced them. Terms that were never used in any merge are prime. On the next round the dashes must sit in the same places, otherwise the two terms are not neighbours. The chart step is the K-map's 'essential' test: a minterm covered by exactly one prime forces that prime into every cover. The method gives exactly the same answer as the map, with no drawing.

examples.setup: Apply Quine-McCluskey to F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(2, 3, 8, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15).
steps: Write the minterms in binary and group by number of 1s: one 1: 2 (0010), 8 (1000). Two 1s: 3 (0011), 10 (1010), 12 (1100). Three 1s: 13 (1101), 14 (1110). Four 1s: 15 (1111).
Merge again, with dashes in the same places: 8,10,12,14 = 1--0 (from 8,10 with 12,14) and 12,13,14,15 = 11-- (from 12,13 with 14,15). No more merges.
Terms that never merged are prime: 001- (A′B′C), -010 (B′CD′), 1--0 (AD′) and 11-- (AB). That is four prime implicants.
Chart: m3 appears only in 001-, so A′B′C is essential; AD′ owns m8 and AB owns m13; B′CD′ covers only m2 and m10, which are already covered. F = A′B′C + AD′ + AB.
examples.answer: Primes: A′B′C, B′CD′, AD′, AB. Minimal F = A′B′C + AD′ + AB.

examples.setup: Which pair of minterms of a 4-variable function can merge in the first pass: 6 and 14, 6 and 9, or 4 and 11? What term results?
steps: Two minterms merge only if their binary forms differ in exactly one bit.
6 = 0110 and 14 = 1110 differ only in the first bit. They can merge: −110, which is BCD′.
6 = 0110 and 9 = 1001 differ in all four bits. No.
4 = 0100 and 11 = 1011 differ in all four bits. No.
Quick test: the numbers of 1s must differ by exactly 1 (6 has two 1s and 14 has three), and then the XOR must be a power of two (6 XOR 14 = 8).
examples.answer: 6 and 14 merge, giving −110 = BCD′.

examples.setup: In the basic example, how many prime implicants does the method list, and how many are essential?
steps: The unmerged terms are 001-, -010, 1--0 and 11--: four prime implicants.
Chart check: m3 is only in A′B′C, m8 only in AD′ (also m10, m12, m14 are shared), m13 only in AB (also m12, m14, m15 shared).
m2 is in A′B′C and B′CD′; m10 is in B′CD′ and AD′. Both are covered by essentials already.
So 4 primes, 3 essential. B′CD′ is a prime that the minimal answer does not need.
examples.answer: 4 prime implicants, 3 essential.

cards.title: Cost of an expression
cards.simple: Two kinds of cost show up in questions. The first is the number of literals, the letters in the final formula. The second is the number of gates in a circuit. If the circuit must use only NOR gates, you first write the answer as a product of sums. Then you use one NOR gate for each bracket that has two or more letters, and one last NOR gate to join them all. A bracket with a single letter needs no gate of its own. The count depends on the form you minimised, so always use the one the circuit needs. In exam words: cost = literals of the minimal form; for NOR-only circuits take the minimal POS, with one NOR per multi-literal sum term plus one output NOR (complements available).
cards.idea: **Cost** is the number of **literals** of the minimal form, or the number of **gates**. For a NOR-only circuit, minimise the **POS**, use one NOR per sum term with two or more literals, and one more NOR to combine them.
cards.definition:
- Literal cost: total number of variable occurrences in the minimal SOP (or POS).
- NOR-NOR realisation of a POS with $s$ sum terms, $s_1$ of them with two or more literals (complements available, gates of any size): $s_1+1$ gates.
- Single-literal sum terms feed straight into the output NOR (use the complemented input).
- If complements are not available, add one NOT (a NOR with tied inputs) per complemented literal needed.
- NAND-NAND is the same for an SOP.
cards.intuition_full: Costs are counted on the minimal form because that is the cheapest circuit of that type. A NOR gate outputs 1 only when all its inputs are 0, so NOR(x, y) = (x + y)′ is the complement of the sum. The output NOR then takes the complements of the sums and gives (s1′ + s2′ + ...)′ = s1·s2·..., which is the product of the sums. That is why a POS maps to NOR-NOR. A sum term with a single literal t would need a NOR with one input, giving t′; but t′ is just the complement of the input, so it can be wired directly if complemented inputs are available. When the question says 'inputs and their complements are available', the NOT gates are free. When it does not, each complemented literal needs an inverter, which can be built as a NOR with its inputs tied. Gate-size assumptions (2-input only or any number of inputs) must be read from the question, since they change the count.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = (A + B)(C + D)(A′ + D′). Find the minimal POS literals and the NOR gates for a NOR-NOR circuit (complements available, gates of any size). Compare with the minimal SOP.
steps: The ones of F are 5, 6, 7, 10, 14. Its zeros are the other eleven cells.
Group the zeros: column CD = 00 (cells 0, 4, 12, 8) gives C′D′; row AB = 00 (cells 0, 1, 3, 2) gives A′B′; the block A = 1, D = 1 (cells 9, 11, 13, 15) gives AD.
F′ = C′D′ + A′B′ + AD. Complement: F = (C + D)(A + B)(A′ + D′), with 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 literals.
NOR realisation: one NOR for each of the three sums, giving (C+D)′, (A+B)′ and (A′+D′)′. One output NOR combines the three complements into the product of the sums.
Gate count: 3 + 1 = 4 NOR gates. The minimal SOP of F costs 9 literals, so the POS is the cheaper form here.
examples.answer: 6 literals and 4 NOR gates; the SOP needs 9 literals.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 3). Inputs and their complements are available, and NOR gates have 2 inputs. How many NOR gates realise F?
steps: Group the zeros: row A = 1 (cells 4, 5, 6, 7) gives A; the pair {2, 6} (B = 1, C = 0) gives BC′. F′ = A + BC′.
F = A′(B′ + C): the POS has two sum terms, A′ (one literal) and (B′ + C) (two literals).
The two-literal sum needs one NOR: NOR(B′, C) = (B′ + C)′. The single literal A′ needs no gate: feed A (the complement of the term) into the output NOR.
Output NOR(A, NOR(B′, C)) = A′(B′ + C) = F. Two gates, both 2-input.
examples.answer: 2 NOR gates.

examples.setup: In the basic example, the circuit needs the complemented literals A′ and D′. What if complements are not available?
steps: The sum (A′ + D′) is built as NOR(A′, D′), so it needs the signals A′ and D′.
Each complement needs an inverter. An inverter is a NOR gate with both inputs tied: NOR(A, A) = A′.
Two inverters are required, one for A and one for D.
Total = 4 + 2 = 6 NOR gates.
examples.answer: 6 NOR gates when complements are not available.

cards.title: Counting prime and essential implicants
cards.simple: Counting questions ask: how many maximal groups are there, and how many of them are unavoidable? List every maximal group first. Then build a little chart with the groups down the side and the real 1s across the top, and put a mark where a group covers a 1. If a 1 has only one mark in its column, the group owning that mark is essential. Don't-care cells are treated as 1s for making groups bigger, but they do not get a column, because nobody has to cover them. Some functions, with a ring of groups, have no essential group at all. In exam words: list all prime implicants (treating X as 1), then count those with a private real 1; cyclic maps have none.
cards.idea: **List** every prime implicant (X counts as 1). Make a **chart** of primes against the real 1s. A column with a single mark makes that prime **essential**. Don't-cares have no column, so they cannot make a prime essential.
cards.definition:
Counting recipe:

1. Find all prime implicants, using X cells as 1s.
2. Draw the chart: one column per real 1 (not per X), one row per prime.
3. A column with exactly one mark gives an essential prime.
4. Number of essential primes = number of distinct primes marked in such columns.

- Primes that cover only X cells are never essential.
- A cyclic function can have many primes and no essential one.
cards.intuition_full: The chart is the formal version of 'who owns each 1'. A real 1 must be covered, so if only one prime covers it, that prime is forced into every cover, which is the definition of essential. Don't-cares need no cover, so they never create such an obligation; they only add more primes (bigger groups), which usually removes ownership of a 1 and can make fewer primes essential. A prime that covers only X cells is legal but useless. Counting both numbers is a common exam form because it checks the whole method: you have to enlarge groups with X cells, count the primes correctly, and then test each real 1. An organised list prevents the usual errors: a missed wrap-around group, a non-maximal group counted as prime, or an X cell treated as a real 1 in the chart.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 14) + d(0, 1, 5, 15). Count the prime implicants and the essential ones.
steps: Treat the X cells as 1s and find the maximal groups. The primes are BD (5, 7, 13, 15), BC (6, 7, 14, 15), A′C′D (1, 5), A′B′C′ (0, 1), ACD (11, 15) and AB (12, 13, 14, 15). Six primes.
Chart: one column per real 1 (6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 14). Marks: BD covers 7 and 13; BC covers 6, 7, 14; ACD covers 11; AB covers 12, 13, 14. A′C′D and A′B′C′ cover no real 1.
Columns with one mark: m6 (only BC), m11 (only ACD), m12 (only AB). So BC, ACD and AB are essential.
BD is not essential: m7 and m13 are also covered by BC and AB. A′C′D and A′B′C′ cover only don't-cares, so they are never essential.
Count: 6 primes, 3 essential. The essentials alone cover all six real 1s: F = BC + ACD + AB.
examples.answer: 6 prime implicants, 3 essential.

examples.setup: Same chart idea, no don't-cares: F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7) is a ring of six pairs. How many primes and how many essential?

Chart: each real 1 lies in exactly two primes (m0 in A′B′ and A′C′; m1 in A′B′ and B′C, and so on).
No column has a single mark, so no prime is essential.
Count: 6 primes, 0 essential. A minimal cover needs 3 of the 6 pairs, and there are two such covers.
examples.answer: 6 prime implicants, 0 essential.

examples.setup: In the basic example, change the don't-cares to ordinary zeros. What happens to the primes and to the cost?

The essentials leave m14 and m6 to be covered: BCD′ covers both. The cheapest cover costs 13 literals, against 7 when the don't-cares were used.

**List** every prime implicant (X counts as 1). Make a **chart** of primes against the real 1s. A column with a single mark makes that prime **essential**. Don't-cares have no column, so they cannot make a prime essential.

Counting recipe:

1. Find all prime implicants, using X cells as 1s.
2. Draw the chart: one column per real 1 (not per X), one row per prime.
3. A column with exactly one mark gives an essential prime.
4. Number of essential primes = number of distinct primes marked in such columns.

- Primes that cover only X cells are never essential.
- A cyclic function can have many primes and no essential one.

**Worked example.** F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 14) + d(0, 1, 5, 15). Count the prime implicants and the essential ones.

1. Treat the X cells as 1s and find the maximal groups. The primes are BD (5, 7, 13, 15), BC (6, 7, 14, 15), A′C′D (1, 5), A′B′C′ (0, 1), ACD (11, 15) and AB (12, 13, 14, 15). Six primes.
2. Chart: one column per real 1 (6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 14). Marks: BD covers 7 and 13; BC covers 6, 7, 14; ACD covers 11; AB covers 12, 13, 14. A′C′D and A′B′C′ cover no real 1.
3. Columns with one mark: m6 (only BC), m11 (only ACD), m12 (only AB). So BC, ACD and AB are essential.
4. BD is not essential: m7 and m13 are also covered by BC and AB. A′C′D and A′B′C′ cover only don't-cares, so they are never essential.
5. Count: 6 primes, 3 essential. The essentials alone cover all six real 1s: F = BC + ACD + AB.

**Answer:** 6 prime implicants, 3 essential.

cards.title: Hazard-free covers
cards.simple: In a real circuit a signal does not change instantly, and different paths take slightly different times. Suppose two neighbouring cells of a map are both 1, but they are covered by two different terms. When one input flips, the first term may switch off a moment before the second one switches on. For a tiny moment the output drops to 0 and comes back up, even though it should have stayed at 1. This unwanted blip is called a static-1 hazard. The cure is to add an extra term that covers both neighbouring cells, so one term stays on while the others switch. In exam words: a static-1 hazard exists when two adjacent 1s are not covered by a common product term; a hazard-free SOP adds the bridging (consensus) terms.
cards.idea: A **static-1 hazard** happens when two **adjacent 1s** are covered by **different** terms: the output can glitch to 0 when one input changes. To be **hazard-free**, add a term that covers both cells. A minimal SOP is often not hazard-free.
cards.definition:
- Two 1-cells that differ in one variable are adjacent. A single input change moves between them.
- Static-1 hazard: the output should stay 1 but may briefly become 0. It occurs if no single product term contains both adjacent cells.
- Hazard-free two-level cover: every pair of adjacent 1s is contained in some term of the cover.
- The extra terms are consensus terms; they are redundant for the logic value but needed for the timing.
cards.intuition_full: In a two-level circuit, each product term is an AND gate. When a variable changes, an AND gate that depends on it may turn off while another turns on. If the two gates cover the two different cells of an adjacent pair, there can be a very short time when neither is on, and the OR gate outputs 0. If one term covers both cells, that term stays 1 throughout the change, so the output never dips. That is why the cure is a term that spans the boundary between two groups. On a K-map the boundary is where two separate groups touch along an edge of cells that are both 1. The minimal SOP deliberately avoids redundant terms, so it often leaves such boundaries unbridged, while a hazard-free cover pays for the extra safety with extra literals. The glitch problem only concerns single input changes between two 1s.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C) = Σm(0, 1, 5, 7). The minimal SOP is A′B′ + AC. Is it free of static-1 hazards?
steps: Map the ones: 0 and 1 (row A = 0), 5 and 7 (row A = 1). Groups: A′B′ = {0, 1} and AC = {5, 7}. This is the minimal SOP, 4 literals.
Look for adjacent ones in different groups: cells 1 (001) and 5 (101) are adjacent (they differ in A only), and 1 is covered only by A′B′, 5 only by AC.
Change A from 0 to 1 with B = 0, C = 1. A′B′ turns off while AC turns on. If AC lags, the output dips to 0 for a moment: a static-1 hazard.
Add the term that covers both cells: B′C (cells 1 and 5). Now F = A′B′ + AC + B′C.
The extra term B′C stays on during the change, so there is no glitch. Cost: 6 literals instead of 4.
examples.answer: Not hazard-free. F = A′B′ + AC + B′C is hazard-free.

examples.setup: F(A, B, C, D) = Σm(0, 1, 5, 7, 15). One minimal SOP is A′B′C′ + A′BD + BCD. Is it hazard-free? If not, which term is missing?
steps: List the adjacent pairs of ones (cells that differ in one bit): (0, 1), (1, 5), (5, 7) and (7, 15).
Check each pair for a term that contains both cells. (0, 1): A′B′C′ has both. (5, 7): A′BD has both. (7, 15): BCD has both.
Pair (1, 5) has no common term: cell 1 is only in A′B′C′, cell 5 only in A′BD. A hazard can occur when B changes.
Cells 1 and 5 differ only in B, so the bridge is A′C′D (A = 0, C = 0, D = 1). It contains both cells.
Hazard-free cover: A′B′C′ + A′BD + BCD + A′C′D. Trap avoided: only the pair that lacks a common term needs a bridge.
examples.answer: Not hazard-free. Add A′C′D.

examples.setup: Does adding a bridge term change the logic function?
steps: The bridge term B′C in the basic example covers cells 1 and 5, which are already 1 in F.
So it does not change any output value: the function is the same.
It is a consensus term: A′B′ and AC have consensus B′C.
The change is only in timing: the hazard-free circuit has an extra AND gate and extra literals.
examples.answer: No. The function is unchanged; only the glitch behaviour improves.

cards.why: Hazards are why real logic cannot always use the minimal SOP. In GATE: decide which cover(s) guarantee no glitch, or which extra term is needed.
how: Mark the ones and the groups of the cover.
List every pair of adjacent 1s.
For each pair, check some single term contains both cells.
For any pair that fails, add a term covering both.
cards.mistake: Calling the minimal SOP hazard-free. It usually lacks the bridging term. Another slip is adding bridge terms for pairs that are already inside one group; only the pairs split between groups need one.
edge_cases: Two groups that only touch at a corner (differing in two variables) need no bridge.
Hazard-free covers are not minimal: they have extra, redundant terms.
A static-0 hazard concerns adjacent zeros in a POS and is the dual.
Hazards matter only for single-input changes.
connections: Consensus terms: dl.boolean_min, card b1 (the redundant yz in xy + x′z + yz).
Prime implicants: card k4; every prime of the function is a candidate bridge.
Foundations: **Sets and logic** (found.sets_logic) covers the idea of overlapping sets: the bridge term is the overlap region.

Leftover ones: 4, 5 and 6 in row 01. Which primes can cover them?
Two primes of three literals cover them: A′BC′ for 4 and 5, and A′BD′ for 4 and 6 (it wraps across the left and right edges).

scenes.title: Minimal POS by grouping the zeros of Σm(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12)

steps.caption: For a product of sums, look at the zeros: 5, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15.
Group the zeros 5, 7, 13, 15: a 2×2 block where B = 1 and D = 1 stay fixed. Product term BD.
Group the zeros 10, 11, 14, 15: a 2×2 block where A = 1 and C = 1 stay fixed. Product term AC.
Complement with De Morgan: F = (BD + AC)′ = (B′ + D′)(A′ + C′). Each zero-group becomes a sum with complemented variables.
Check a zero, m5: B′ + D′ = 0 + 0 = 0, so F = 0. Check a one, m4: B′ + D′ = 1 and A′ + C′ = 1, so F = 1.
Write the eight minterms in binary and sort them by the number of 1s: one 1 (2, 8), two 1s (3, 10, 12), three (13, 14), four (15).
Compare neighbouring groups. Where one bit differs, merge and write a dash: 2,3 = 001-, 2,10 = -010, 8,10 = 10-0, and six more. Nine merges.
Merge again with dashes in the same places: 8,10 with 12,14 gives 1--0; 12,13 with 14,15 gives 11--. Nothing merges after that.
Terms that never merged are the prime implicants: 001-, -010 (both pairs), and the quads 1--0 and 11--. Four primes.

scenes.title: From zero-groups to a NOR-NOR circuit

steps.caption: F = (A + B)(C + D)(A′ + D′) is 1 only at cells 5, 6, 7, 10 and 14. A NOR-only circuit starts from the product of sums, so we group the zeros.
Zero-groups: column CD = 00 (C′D′), row AB = 00 (A′B′) and the 2×2 block A = 1, D = 1 (AD).
Complement with De Morgan: F = (C + D)(A + B)(A′ + D′). Each sum has two literals: 6 literals in all.
NOR circuit: one NOR for each sum gives its complement; an output NOR combines the three complements into the product.
The output NOR makes it F. Total 3 + 1 = 4 NOR gates (complements available). The SOP form would cost 9 literals.
